description: Welcome to GIS Gynix! We are expereinced in GIS & Remote Sensing with hands on expereince in the field. We are also experience in Python, SQL, React, Node.js, Spatial analysis and machine learning. Our strengths include analytical thinking, problem-solving, identifying patterns in datasets, and turning data into meaningful insights. Join us to combine technology, AI, and agricultural innovation to build a solution which can help our local farmers.
summary:
ZameenDost is a free, bilingual (English and Urdu) Google Earth Engine app that helps Khushab farmers answer two questions: should I water today, and what should I grow next? The farmer clicks their field on the map and answers a few simple questions: crop, sowing date, soil, last irrigation and recent rain.
The app combines NASA data (GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, HLS crop greenness and SRTM terrain) with weather and soil-map data. It runs a standard FAO-56 daily soil-water budget and gives clear advice: irrigate now, soon, or not yet, with the date and pump hours. A second tool compares the current crop rotation with the best alternatives. It shows the reasons, evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks to check locally.
The benefit is less guesswork, water saved, healthier soil and a tool farmers can read in their own language. It supports local judgment and does not replace it.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

ZameenDost is a free Google Earth Engine App that helps farmers in Khushab, Punjab answer two questions: should I water my field today, and what should I grow next?

Water today. The farmer clicks their field on the map (or uses the demo farm) and answers seven simple questions: crop, sowing date, soil, watering before sowing, irrigation since, rain since, and an optional pump question. The app runs a daily soil-water budget based on FAO-56, using rain, weather and a satellite estimate of how much of the field the crop covers. It answers “irrigate now”, “irrigate soon” or “not yet”, with the likely next date, the pump hours needed, the reasons and a confidence level.

Rotation plan. The app compares the farmer’s current rotation with every winter and summer crop pair that fits in a year. It shows the current rotation plus the four best alternatives, ranked by the farmer’s own priorities. For each one it gives the reasons, evidence charts, benefits, information gaps and risks to check locally.

Language. A switch at the top translates the whole interface into Urdu.

What benefits does it have?

  • Replaces guesswork with advice based on NASA and standard FAO data.
  • Helps save irrigation water and pump time.
  • Shows the benefits of rotations: less irrigation, nitrogen from legumes, deeper roots and fewer bare days.
  • Is free, runs in a browser or on a phone, and needs no software.
  • Is honest about uncertainty: it shows confidence, compares three ways of estimating crop water use, and lists what it does not know.

What is the intended impact?

We want small farms in Khushab to irrigate and rotate crops on evidence instead of habit, and to use less water without losing yield. It is built to support a farmer’s own judgment and local advice. The Urdu interface is meant to bring satellite tools to farmers who are usually left out. We have not yet measured real-world impact; the next step is to check the answers against irrigation records from real farms.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Platform: Google Earth Engine Code Editor, published as an Earth Engine App.
  • Language: JavaScript, using Earth Engine’s ee and ui libraries, with Earth Engine charts for the graphs.
  • NASA data: GPM IMERG (rain), SMAP (soil moisture), HLS Landsat and Sentinel-2 (crop cover and moisture) and SRTM (elevation and slope).
  • Other data: ERA5-Land and NOAA GFS (weather and forecast), SoilGrids (soil texture) and Sentinel-2 (additional crop cover).
  • Methods: FAO-56 water balance, Penman-Monteith and Hargreaves evapotranspiration, SAVI-based crop cover (Allen and Pereira 2009).
  • Testing: a Node.js simulation of Earth Engine used to test both languages. No special hardware; a browser or phone is enough.
  • AI assistance: Claude helped write and test the code.

How is it creative?

  • It combines two farm decisions, water today and rotation planning, in one simple tool.
  • It is fully bilingual, with every question, answer, chart and message translated into Urdu.
  • Questions use farm language (rauni, acres, inches, cusecs) instead of technical terms.
  • It cross-checks itself: three ways of estimating crop water use and two weather formulas are compared, and the app says when they disagree.
  • It ranks rotations by what the farmer says matters to them.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Local users: language, literacy and phones, so inputs are dropdowns and the interface is in Urdu.
  • Data limits: weather and rain data cover 10 km or larger cells, so nearby fields can get similar answers. Crop values come from FAO tables, not our farm.
  • Missing information: soil tests, salinity, groundwater, canal turns and prices are not included, and the app says so.
  • Uncertainty: the farmer’s own rain and irrigation reports change the answer, so the app shows how much.
  • Local review: every rotation option lists risks to check with local advisers before any change.
  • Source clarity: the app marks which data is NASA’s and which is not.
